In April 2022 they were finally cut, by Mama Ngina Kenyatta, in a ceremony Muthoni said marked Kenya's full independence. She died in 2023, aged around ninety-two, honoured at last as a national heroine and a living reminder that the fight for freedom was carried, in part, by women the history books had left out.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Muthoni Kirima), The Africa Report, Nation Africa, Standard Media.

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Muthoni Likimani (1926-2023) from Kenya, East Africa. Era: Independence. Causes: Anti-colonial activism, Scholarship & literature, Women's rights, Education. Kenyan writer, broadcaster, and Mau Mau supporter who documented the untold stories of women in Kenya's independence struggle through her groundbreaking book 'Passbook Number F.47927'. Fun fact: Muthoni Likimani documented the untold stories of women in Kenya's independence struggle through her groundbreaking book Passbook Number F.47927.

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Muthoni Likimani was born in 1926 in Kenya during British colonial rule. Educated at mission schools and later in the United Kingdom, she became one of Kenya's first women broadcasters, working for the Voice of Kenya radio station. She was also an entrepreneur, founding a public relations firm that became one of the most successful in East Africa.

But it was as a writer that Likimani made her most enduring contribution. Her best-known work, Passbook Number F.47927: Women and Mau Mau in Kenya (1985), documented the experiences of women during the Mau Mau uprising — stories that had been almost entirely ignored by male historians and memoirists.

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
Kenya's Mau Mau uprising (1952–1960) was a pivotal moment in the country's struggle for independence. While the male fighters in the forests received most of the historical attention, women played equally critical — and often more dangerous — roles as intelligence gatherers, supply runners, oath administrators, and keepers of the home front under brutal colonial emergency regulations.

The British colonial government imposed a passbook system that controlled the movement of African Kenyans. Women were subjected to forced communal labour, detention, and collective punishment. Despite this, their stories were largely absent from the historical record until writers like Likimani insisted on telling them.

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Muthoni Likimani fought to ensure that women's contributions to Kenya's independence were not erased from history. Passbook Number F.47927 was a pioneering work of creative non-fiction that gave voice to the women who had endured the passbook system, detention camps, and the daily terror of colonial emergency rule.

Beyond writing, she used her broadcasting platform to advocate for women's education and empowerment, and she supported women's entrepreneurship through her business career. She was a fierce advocate for the recognition of Mau Mau veterans, many of whom were never compensated for their sacrifices.

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Authored Passbook Number F.47927: Women and Mau Mau in Kenya, a landmark text in African women's history
- One of Kenya's first women radio broadcasters at Voice of Kenya
- Founded a successful public relations firm in Nairobi
- Lifelong advocate for the recognition of women's roles in the Mau Mau uprising
- Published multiple novels and non-fiction works on Kenyan women's experiences
- Awarded national honours for her contributions to Kenyan literature and culture

chunks.title: Muthoni Likimani
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Muthoni Likimani died in 2023 at the age of 97. Her work ensured that the women of the Mau Mau era would not be forgotten. Passbook Number F.47927 remains essential reading in African studies programmes worldwide and has inspired a generation of scholars to investigate the gendered dimensions of African liberation struggles. She proved that telling women's stories is itself an act of liberation.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Muthoni Likimani), Kenya National Archives, Journal of African History

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nadine Gordimer (1923-2014) from South Africa, Southern Africa. Era: Colonial. Causes: Anti-apartheid resistance, Literature & free expression, Human rights, Political freedom. South African novelist and short-story writer. Nobel Prize in Literature (1991); used her work to oppose apartheid and to explore race, power, and moral responsibility. Fun fact: Nadine Gordimer won the 1991 Nobel Prize in Literature for decades of writing that opposed apartheid and explored race, power, and moral responsibility.

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nadine Gordimer was born on 20 November 1923 in Springs, South Africa. She published her first story as a teenager and went on to write novels and short fiction that examined life under apartheid. She was banned and censored by the regime but continued to write and to support the liberation movement.

She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991 — the first South African to receive it — for, in the words of the Academy, her "magnificent epic writing" that "has been of very great benefit to humanity." She remained politically engaged after apartheid and spoke out on HIV/AIDS, censorship, and freedom of expression.

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Under apartheid, many white South Africans benefited from or accepted the system. Gordimer used her position and her art to expose its cruelty and to side with the oppressed. Her books were read worldwide and helped shape international understanding of South Africa.

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Nadine Gordimer fought apartheid through literature and activism. She joined the ANC when it was still banned, hid activists, and used her international stature to support the struggle. She advocated for free speech, human rights, and moral clarity.

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Nobel Prize in Literature (1991)
- Author of The Conservationist, July's People, Burger's Daughter, and many short stories
- Member of the ANC; supported the anti-apartheid movement at home and abroad
- Honoured globally for literature and human rights

chunks.title: Nadine Gordimer
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nadine Gordimer died on 13 July 2014. She is remembered as one of the 20th century’s great writers and as a conscience of South Africa who refused to look away from injustice.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nadine Gordimer), Nobel Prize

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nana Asma'u (1793-1864) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Pre-Colonial. Causes: Women's education, Scholarship & literature, Religious leadership, Cultural preservation. Scholar, poet, and educator in the Sokoto Caliphate who built one of the earliest known systems of women's education in West Africa, training female teachers who carried learning into rural communities. Fun fact: Nana Asma'u built one of the earliest known systems of women's education in West Africa, training female teachers to carry learning into rural communities across the Sokoto Caliphate.

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nana Asma'u bint Usman dan Fodio was born in 1793 in what is now northern Nigeria, the daughter of Usman dan Fodio, founder of the Sokoto Caliphate. She was raised in a household that valued scholarship for women and men equally. She was fluent in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa, and Tamacheq, and began writing poetry and religious commentary as a young woman.

She was not a figurehead. She was a working scholar who produced a body of written work spanning decades: poems, historical chronicles, elegies, and instructional texts used to educate women across the caliphate.

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: The Sokoto Caliphate, established after the Fulani jihad of 1804, was one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa. While women in many parts of the world were denied formal education, the caliphate's founding ideology held that educating women was a religious obligation. Nana Asma'u operated within this framework, but she pushed it further than anyone before her.

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Nana Asma'u created the Yan Taru ("those who congregate"), a network of itinerant female teachers called jajis who travelled to rural communities to teach women who could not come to the capital. Each jaji carried Asma'u's poems and teaching materials. The system reached thousands of women across the caliphate.

She wrote works on Islamic law, theology, and history. She composed elegies for fallen leaders and poems that documented the political and military events of her time. She used poetry as a teaching tool, writing in local languages so women who did not read Arabic could still learn.

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Created the Yan Taru, one of the earliest documented women's education networks in West Africa
- Authored over 60 surviving works in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa, and Tamacheq
- Served as a political and intellectual advisor within the Sokoto Caliphate
- Her educational methods are studied as a model for community-based learning
- Recognised by UNESCO and scholars of Islamic feminism as a pioneering educator

chunks.title: Nana Asma'u
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nana Asma'u is claimed by multiple traditions: Islamic scholars cite her as proof that women's education is central to Muslim life; African historians hold her up as evidence of sophisticated pre-colonial intellectual culture; feminists around the world point to her as a woman who built institutions, not just ideas.

Her name is carried by schools and scholarships across Nigeria. The Yan Taru model is studied in development and education circles to this day.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nana Asma'u), Beverly Mack and Jean Boyd, One Woman's Jihad, Encyclopædia Britannica

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings (born 1948, still living) from Ghana, West Africa. Era: Modern. Causes: Women's political participation, Democracy, Social development, First ladies' activism. Former First Lady of Ghana (1982–2001). Founded the 31st December Women's Movement; ran for president in 2016; advocate for women's empowerment and development. Fun fact: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings founded the 31st December Women's Movement and later ran for the presidency of Ghana in 2016.

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings was born in 1948. She married Jerry John Rawlings, who led Ghana as head of state and later as elected president from 1981 to 2001. As First Lady she did not limit herself to ceremonial roles.

In 1982 she founded the 31st December Women’s Movement (DWM), which grew into one of Ghana’s largest women’s organisations, promoting literacy, livelihoods, and political participation. She later entered party politics and in 2016 became the first woman to run for president on a major party ticket in Ghana.

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Ghana’s Fourth Republic began in 1992. Nana Konadu used her platform to push for women’s rights and social programmes. Her presidential run highlighted both the possibility and the obstacles for women in top office.

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Nana Konadu fought for women’s political and economic empowerment, girls’ education, and community development. The DWM worked on health, microfinance, and advocacy. She has been a vocal figure in Ghanaian politics and women’s organising.

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- First Lady of Ghana (1982–2001)
- Founded the 31st December Women’s Movement (1982)
- First woman to run for president in Ghana (2016, NDP)
- Influential voice in Ghanaian women’s and development politics

chunks.title: Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nana Konadu Rawlings is remembered for turning the role of First Lady into a vehicle for mass organising and for paving the way for future women presidential candidates in Ghana.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nana Konadu Agyeman Rawlings)

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nawal El Moutawakel (born 1962, still living) from Morocco, North Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Women in sport, Olympic leadership, Youth empowerment through sport. The Moroccan hurdler who won the first ever women's 400m hurdles at the 1984 Olympics, becoming the first Moroccan, Arab, African, and Muslim woman to take Olympic gold, then rose to the top of world sport as an IOC Vice President. Fun fact: After her 1984 victory, King Hassan II declared that every baby girl born in Morocco that day would be named Nawal.

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
August 8, 1984. Los Angeles. A 22-year-old from Casablanca settles into her blocks for a race no woman has ever run at the Olympics. She is 5 feet 1 inch tall. She is the only woman on Morocco's entire Olympic team. "I was really scared," she remembered later. "I was the only female athlete in the all Moroccan delegation, and everybody was counting on me." Fifty-four point six one seconds later, Nawal El Moutawakel crossed the line more than half a second clear of the field, and history split into before and after.

She grew up in a sports-mad family in Casablanca: her father was a judoka, her mother played volleyball, her siblings ran track. She started running at 14, with her father cheering her on at training when many fathers would not have. In 1983 she won a scholarship to Iowa State University in the United States to study physical education and physiotherapy. Before she left, her father told her: "You've won everything, you still have to win this Olympic gold." He died suddenly three months before the race, and because she was far from home, she only learned the news a month later. She turned grief into fuel. "I used this as a force, saying to myself in the mirror, you should win for your father because he let you leave, because he believed in you."

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Biography (2)
chunks.text:
Her win was Morocco's first Olympic gold medal of any kind, and it made her the first Moroccan, the first Arab woman, the first woman from an African nation, and the first Muslim woman ever to win Olympic gold. King Hassan II telephoned her personally, then declared that all girls born in Morocco on the day of her victory would carry her name. When she flew home, the party stretched for miles: "It was a huge celebration from the airport to the highway all the way through my city Casablanca."

Knee surgery ended her racing career at 25, but not her race. She became a coach, an organizer, and then one of the most powerful people in world sport: a council member of the international athletics federation from 1995, an IOC member from 1998, Morocco's Minister of Sports in 2007, a member of the IOC executive board from 2008, and IOC Vice President from 2012 to 2016, re-elected in 2024.

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
When Nawal lined up in Los Angeles, the women's 400m hurdles was brand new to the Olympics. As she put it herself, it was "a highly technical event which at the international level was only a men's event." The 1984 Games were a turning point for women's athletics generally, but women from North Africa and the Muslim world were barely represented at all. Many countries had never sent a woman to the Olympics, and a Moroccan girl who ran in shorts on a public track was defying more than gravity.

Morocco in the 1980s was a young nation under King Hassan II, hungry for symbols of achievement on the world stage. Sport was one of the few arenas where a developing country could beat wealthy powers head to head. That is why one woman's 54.61 seconds mattered so much: it was not just a medal, it was proof, broadcast worldwide, of what a Moroccan woman could do.

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
The turning point of Nawal's life was also a test of everything her father had given her. He was the one who let her run, let her travel alone to America, and set her the impossible goal of Olympic gold. Then he was gone, three months before the biggest race of her life. She could have collapsed. Instead she stood in front of the mirror and made his belief her engine. When she won, she was not just the fastest woman over ten hurdles. She was an answer to every voice that said girls like her should stay home.

She understood immediately that her medal belonged to more than herself. She had noticed, even in 1984, that there were no women journalists in her country's delegation. So she spent the next four decades prying open doors. As a sports official she pushed for women in every federation, in every sport, in every boardroom. "Countries whose women never attended Olympic Games," she observed, "were attending to win."

The proof came in Paris in 2024, the first Olympics with full gender parity among athletes, a goal she had worked toward inside the IOC for years. "We will witness for the first time now in Paris 2024, almost, equal opportunities for women in every field," she said. "This is the happiest moment for me."

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Won the first ever women's 400m hurdles at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics in 54.61 seconds, Morocco's first Olympic gold medal
- First Moroccan, Arab, African, and Muslim woman to win Olympic gold
- Became a council member of the international athletics federation (now World Athletics) in 1995 and a member of the International Olympic Committee in 1998
- Served as Morocco's Minister of Sports from 2007
- Joined the IOC executive board in 2008, the first Muslim woman to do so, and served as IOC Vice President from 2012 to 2016, re-elected in 2024
- Led IOC commissions overseeing Olympic host cities, including chairing the Coordination Commission for Rio 2016, and carried the Olympic flag at the Turin 2006 opening ceremony

chunks.title: Nawal El Moutawakel
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Somewhere in Morocco there are women in their early forties named Nawal because of one race in Los Angeles. That royal decree made her victory a living, breathing legacy, written into birth certificates. More broadly, her win told girls across Africa and the Muslim world that the Olympic podium was theirs too. Generations of champions, from Algeria to Bahrain to Ethiopia, came of age with her image as proof of possibility.

Inside world sport, she moved from symbol to architect. As one of the highest-ranking women in Olympic history, she helped drive the movement toward gender equality that culminated in the fifty-fifty athlete split at Paris 2024, and she continues to shape the Games as part of the team preparing Los Angeles 2028, the city where it all began. From a lone woman in a national delegation to a Vice President of the Olympic movement: few athletes have ever cleared higher hurdles.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nawal El Moutawakel); World Athletics Heritage, "Nawal El Moutawakel: the 54 seconds that changed her life"; Yahoo Sports, "Changed the Game: Nawal El Moutawakel's stunning gold medal broke barrier for Muslim athletes"; The Olympic Museum via Google Arts & Culture; Olympics.com.

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nawal El Saadawi (1931-2021) from Egypt, North Africa. Era: Modern. Causes: Feminism, Women's rights, Anti-FGM, Secularism, Political freedom. Egyptian feminist writer, psychiatrist, and activist who spent five decades fighting patriarchy, religious conservatism, and female genital mutilation at great personal cost: losing her job, being imprisoned, and living under death threats. Author of over 50 books translated into more than 30 languages. Called 'the Simone de Beauvoir of the Arab world.' Fun fact: Nawal El Saadawi authored over 50 books translated into more than 30 languages, earning her the title 'the Simone de Beauvoir of the Arab world.'

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nawal El Saadawi was born on 27 October 1931 in Kafr Tahla, a village in the Nile Delta, Egypt. Growing up in a rural setting shaped her understanding of the conditions most Egyptian women lived under: conditions of poverty, lack of education, early marriage, and female genital mutilation (FGM). She refused to accept those conditions as natural or inevitable.

She trained as a physician at Cairo University, graduating in 1955, and went on to specialise in psychiatry. She rose to become Director of Public Health at the Egyptian Ministry of Health. But her professional career was about to become a battleground.

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
Egypt in the 1950s–1970s was undergoing rapid modernisation under Nasser and Sadat, but the position of women, particularly regarding sexuality, bodily autonomy, and political participation, remained profoundly constrained. Religious conservatism and patriarchal norms were deeply embedded in law, medicine, and culture. FGM was widely practised and rarely discussed publicly. Women who raised these issues did so at serious professional and personal risk.

Nawal El Saadawi raised them anyway.

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
In 1972, El Saadawi published Women and Sex (Al-Mar'a wa-l-Jins), a medical and social analysis of women's bodies, sexuality, and the damage done by FGM and patriarchal culture. The book was explosive. The Egyptian Medical Association revoked her position at the Ministry of Health. She was dismissed from her job. The book was banned.

She kept writing. Over the following decades she produced more than 50 books (novels, memoirs, essays, and academic work) that systematically dissected the intersections of religion, sex, power, and women's oppression in the Arab world. Her novel Woman at Point Zero (1975), based on interviews she conducted in Qanatir Prison with women on death row, became one of the most widely read Arabic feminist novels in the world.

In 1981, President Sadat had her imprisoned for three months without charge. She wrote about the experience in Memoirs from the Women's Prison. Under Mubarak, she lived under death threats from Islamist groups and was kept on a government "death list."

She co-founded the Arab Women's Solidarity Association in 1982, which was later shut down by the Egyptian government. She continued to speak, write, and travel, unsilenced.

In 2011, at age 79, she went to Tahrir Square during the Egyptian Revolution and took part in the protests. She said simply: it was her duty.

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Author of more than 50 books in Arabic, translated into more than 30 languages
- Woman at Point Zero (1975): landmark feminist novel
- The Hidden Face of Eve (1977): foundational text on women in the Arab world
- Women and Sex (1972): banned; cost her her career; changed Arab feminist discourse permanently
- Co-founder, Arab Women's Solidarity Association (1982)
- Catalonia International Prize, 2003
- North–South Prize of the Council of Europe, 2004
- Honorary doctorates from universities worldwide including University of Chicago, University of York
- BBC 100 Women (2015)

chunks.title: Nawal El Saadawi
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nawal El Saadawi died on 21 March 2021, aged 89. She had never stopped writing, speaking, or demanding. Her work created the vocabulary for Arab feminist discourse and gave generations of women in Egypt and across the region permission to name what had been done to them and to demand something different. Egypt has still not banned FGM absolutely. But the conversation she forced into the open in 1972 cannot be closed.

She was ferocious, uncompromising, and irreplaceable.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nawal El Saadawi), Encyclopædia Britannica, The Guardian, Zed Books (publisher), Al Jazeera

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj (1810-1860) from Senegal, West Africa. Era: Colonial. Causes: Anti-colonial resistance, Political leadership, Sovereignty & independence, Women's leadership. The last great queen of Waalo in northern Senegal, who governed, taxed and went to war against French expansion in the 1850s. Defeated but never forgotten, she is one of Senegal's enduring symbols of resistance and female sovereignty. Fun fact: She left an actual paper trail of defiance: a surviving 1847 letter in which she told the French governor plainly that the kingdom of Waalo was not his to take.

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj was born around 1810 into the ruling Mbodj dynasty of Waalo, a Wolof kingdom in the lower Senegal River valley. Waalo gave its queens, its Lingeer, real power, and Ndaté Yalla inherited it fully. She was crowned Lingeer at the capital, Nder, on 1 October 1846, following her sister Ndjeumbeut, and she ruled with genuine political and military authority at a moment when her kingdom was being squeezed from every side.

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: The Turning Point
chunks.text: By the 1850s the French governor Louis Faidherbe was pushing hard to seize Waalo and the river trade that ran through it. Ndaté Yalla refused to yield her kingdom's sovereignty. She had already written to the French, years earlier, with a bluntness that still startles: Saint-Louis might belong to the Governor and Cayor to its ruler, she wrote, but Waalo belonged to its own king. In February 1855 her armies met Faidherbe's guns in the field. Waalo was overwhelmed, the capital Nder was burned, and the kingdom was annexed, ending centuries of independence. Even in defeat she had done what few dared, telling an advancing colonial power to its face that her land was not for the taking.

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: The 1850s were the decisive decade of French conquest in Senegal, driven from the coastal base at Saint-Louis by Faidherbe's drive to control the gum and grain trade of the river. Waalo, caught between French firepower downstream and Moorish raiders from the north, was the first major Wolof kingdom to fall. Ndaté Yalla's stand was the closing act of its independent history, and her son Sidya carried the resistance on until his own capture and exile.

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Crowned Lingeer (queen) of Waalo in 1846 and ruled with full political and military power
- Organised armed resistance against both French colonial expansion and Trarza Moorish raids
- Asserted Waalo's sovereignty in writing directly to the French governor, a rare first-person act of defiance from a 19th-century African monarch
- Remembered across Senegal as a foremost anti-colonial heroine, with a statue in Dagana and schools that carry her name

chunks.title: Ndaté Yalla Mbodj
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Ndaté Yalla died in 1860, but her name never left Senegalese memory. A statue of her stands in Dagana, schools and even boats carry her name, and she appears in almost every account of Africa's great queens. In a history of conquest that so often erased the women who fought it, she is remembered precisely because she wrote her refusal down and made the record impossible to ignore.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Ndaté Yalla Mbodj), Afrolegends (her 1847 correspondence), Senegalese historical archives.

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana (1840-1898) from Zimbabwe, Southern Africa. Era: Colonial. Causes: Anti-colonial activism, Sovereignty & independence, Spiritual leadership. Zimbabwean spirit medium and revolutionary leader who commanded the First Chimurenga uprising against British colonisation. Her last words, 'my bones will rise,' became the rallying cry of Zimbabwe's independence movement 80 years later. Fun fact: Nehanda's last words before execution — 'my bones will rise' — became the rallying cry of Zimbabwe's independence movement 80 years later.

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana, also known as Mbuya Nehanda, was born around 1840 in Chishawasha, Mashonaland, in the territory that is now Zimbabwe. She was a svikiro, a spirit medium believed to be possessed by Nehanda, a powerful female ancestral spirit of the Shona people.

Among the Zezuru Shona, spirit mediums held enormous authority: they advised chiefs, settled disputes, and communicated the will of the ancestors. Nehanda was not a queen in the European sense. She was something more difficult to understand from the outside, and more dangerous from the inside: a woman through whom the ancestors spoke.

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
In 1889, Cecil John Rhodes' British South Africa Company arrived in Mashonaland, claiming land by treaty and by force. The Shona people, who had governed the region for centuries, found their cattle seized, their labour conscripted, and their land appropriated for white settlers.

The administrator Henry Harwood Polling was particularly brutal in extracting taxes and labour from Shona communities in Nehanda's area. He became a direct target.

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
In 1896–1897, Nehanda became one of the spiritual and military leaders of the First Chimurenga, the uprising of the Shona and Ndebele peoples against British colonial rule. She organised communities, provided spiritual authority to fighters, and is credited with directing the killing of Polling.

She fought for the return of land, the expulsion of colonial forces, and the right of her people to govern themselves under their own law and tradition. The uprising was eventually suppressed by British forces with superior weapons.

Nehanda was captured in 1897. When offered a reprieve if she converted to Christianity, she refused. She was hanged in Salisbury (now Harare) on 27 April 1898.

Her reported last words were: "My bones will rise again."

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Led one of the earliest armed resistance movements against British colonisation in southern Africa
- Her spiritual authority united communities across Mashonaland in organised resistance
- Became the defining symbol of Zimbabwean nationalist identity and liberation struggle
- Her name and image became central to the Second Chimurenga, Zimbabwe's independence war of the 1970s

chunks.title: Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Eighty years after her execution, guerrilla fighters in Zimbabwe's liberation war invoked Nehanda's name and spirit for courage. Songs were written about her. The liberation movement carried her memory the way soldiers carry flags.

In 2021, Zimbabwe unveiled a large statue of Nehanda in central Harare. In a country where most public statues are of colonial figures, her presence in the capital is a statement.

Her bones, as she promised, did rise.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nehanda Charwe Nyakasikana), Zimbabwe National Archives, Encyclopædia Britannica

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah (born 1952, still living) from Namibia, Southern Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: National liberation and independence, Women in political leadership, Peace, stability and clean government. Namibian freedom fighter and veteran diplomat, known simply as NNN, who joined SWAPO at 14, survived arrest and exile under apartheid rule, and in March 2025 became Namibia's first female president, leading a country where women also held the vice presidency and the Speaker's chair. Fun fact: She joined the liberation movement at 14, and 59 years later was sworn in as Namibia's first woman president on the country's Independence Day.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
On 21 March 2025, Namibia's 35th Independence Day, a 72 year old woman raised her right hand and took the presidential oath. Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, known to the whole country by three letters, NNN, had waited most of a lifetime for that moment. She had joined the fight for Namibia's freedom at 14. Now she was its first woman president, and with Vice President Lucia Witbooi beside her and former prime minister Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila in the Speaker's chair, Namibia became one of the very few nations on Earth with women holding the presidency, the vice presidency and the speakership at once.

Netumbo Ndemupelila Nandi was born on 29 October 1952 in Onamutai village in northern Namibia, the ninth of 13 children of an Anglican clergyman. Her country was then called South West Africa and was ruled by apartheid South Africa. In 1966, at 14, she joined SWAPO, the South West Africa People's Organisation, which that year began its armed struggle for independence. By her early twenties she was chairing SWAPO's Youth League in the north. The regime noticed. In 1973 she was arrested for her political activity and given a suspended sentence, and in 1974 she slipped into exile.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Biography (2)
chunks.text: Exile became her education. She worked at SWAPO's headquarters in Lusaka, Zambia, represented the movement in Central and East Africa, trained in Moscow, and later earned a master's degree in diplomatic studies at Keele University in Britain. She returned home in 1989 to help deliver the UN-supervised elections, and after independence in 1990 began three decades of unbroken service: deputy foreign minister, minister for women's affairs, information, environment and tourism, then foreign minister from 2012, deputy prime minister from 2015, and in February 2024, after President Hage Geingob's death, Namibia's first female vice president. In the election of November 2024 she won the presidency with about 58 percent of the vote, more than double her nearest rival.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
Namibia's road to freedom was one of Africa's longest. Colonised by Germany in the 1880s, the territory suffered the genocide of the Herero and Nama peoples, then passed to South African rule after the First World War. Pretoria extended apartheid to the territory and clung to it in defiance of the United Nations for decades. For a village girl in the north, the liberation movement was everywhere: churches, schools and families all fed SWAPO's ranks. Joining at 14 was dangerous, and thousands of young Namibians like Netumbo ended up in prison cells or in exile in Zambia, Tanzania, the Soviet Union and beyond.

Independence finally came on 21 March 1990. SWAPO moved from liberation movement to governing party and has won every election since. But the generation of fighters was ageing, the economy leaned heavily on minerals, and youth unemployment was biting. By 2024 many young Namibians, born free, were demanding results rather than war stories. The election that made Nandi-Ndaitwah president was the closest-fought in the country's history, marked by ballot shortages, extended voting and an opposition court challenge that the Supreme Court dismissed in February 2025. Across the continent, meanwhile, women remained rare at the very top: her victory made her one of only a handful of women ever directly elected to lead an African state.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Nandi-Ndaitwah's first cause was freedom itself. As a teenager she chose a banned movement over a quiet life, and paid with arrest, a criminal sentence and 15 years of exile. The discipline of those years, from Lusaka offices to Moscow classrooms, forged her reputation: devout, precise, incorruptible, a woman who did the work while louder men made speeches.

Her second cause was making independence mean something for women. As minister for women's affairs she pushed gender into national policy; as SWAPO's leadership battles raged, she kept insisting that capability, not gender, should decide who leads. When her moment came, she acted on it. "My election is not only a victory for me, but for every Namibian woman," she said. She cut the cabinet from 21 ministries to 14, filled key portfolios including finance, health and education with women, and international media described the result as one of the world's most gender-balanced governments.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: What She Fought For (2)
chunks.text: The turning point of her story is really a half-century arc: the girl with a suspended sentence in 1973 became the president taking the salute in 2025, in the same country, under a flag she helped raise. At her inauguration she promised more than symbolism: over 500,000 new jobs in five years and free tuition at public universities and technical colleges from 2026. Weeks later she fired a minister facing bribery charges, a signal that "peace and stability", her campaign phrase, included clean hands. "The Namibian nation has voted for peace and stability," she declared after her win. Delivering on that vote is her final fight.

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Elected Namibia's first woman president in November 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote, and inaugurated on 21 March 2025, the 35th anniversary of independence
- Rose from SWAPO Youth League activist at 14, through arrest in 1973 and 15 years of exile, to the highest office in the land
- Served over three decades in government, including as foreign minister (from 2012), deputy prime minister (2015 to 2024) and Namibia's first female vice president (2024 to 2025)
- Appointed a leadership in which women held the vice presidency (Lucia Witbooi), the Speaker's chair (Saara Kuugongelwa-Amadhila) and a large share of a streamlined 14-ministry cabinet
- Pledged and launched flagship programmes including free tertiary education from 2026 and a drive for more than 500,000 new jobs
- Became one of the few women in African history to be directly elected head of state, joining a global handful of countries led simultaneously by women in the top three state offices

chunks.title: Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
For Namibian girls, the change is visible every night on the news: the president, the vice president and the Speaker of the National Assembly are all women. That picture, unthinkable when Netumbo Nandi was born under apartheid rule, quietly resets what a child in Onamutai or Windhoek believes is possible. Regional leaders and international observers now cite Namibia as evidence that liberation politics and women's leadership are not rivals but partners.

Her presidency is still being written. The promises are enormous: half a million jobs, free tertiary education, an oil and gas boom managed from her own office without the corruption that has cursed other producers. Her early moves, a slim cabinet, a fired minister, careful budgets, suggest she intends to be judged on delivery rather than history.

Yet history is already hers. NNN carried a banned movement's membership card at 14, a suspended sentence at 20, an exile's suitcase at 21, a diplomat's portfolio at 60, and the presidential sash at 72. Few leaders anywhere have walked the whole road from colonised child to elected head of state. In Namibia, the road now has her name on it.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah; 2024 Namibian general election); Office of the President of Namibia official biography (op.gov.na); Al Jazeera (3 December 2024); Namibia Economist on the March 2025 cabinet; The EastAfrican and Council on Foreign Relations coverage of the inauguration.

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Ngozi Nwosu (born 1963, still living) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Modern. Causes: Arts & culture, Health awareness, Nollywood, Women's visibility. Nigerian actress; veteran of Nollywood and television. Advocate for health and kidney disease awareness after her own public health journey; beloved for roles in 'Fuji House of Commotion' and others. Fun fact: After her own battle with kidney disease became public, Ngozi Nwosu transformed her personal health journey into a powerful advocacy platform for kidney disease awareness in Nigeria.

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Ngozi Nwosu was born on 17 October 1963 in Abia State, Nigeria. She became one of Nollywood's most recognisable actresses, known for roles in films and in the popular television series Fuji House of Commotion. She has acted in hundreds of productions and is admired for her versatility and longevity in the industry.

In the 2010s she faced a public health crisis related to kidney disease and received support from colleagues and the public. She has since used her platform to raise awareness about kidney health and access to healthcare, and has continued to act and support younger talents.

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Nollywood veterans have often had limited access to health insurance and social protection. Ngozi Nwosu's openness about her health struggles highlighted the need for better support for industry workers and for public awareness of kidney disease and prevention.

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Ngozi Nwosu has fought for health awareness and support for veterans in Nollywood. She has advocated for kidney health, early diagnosis, and access to treatment, and has remained a visible and beloved figure in Nigerian screen culture.

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Veteran actress in Nollywood and television; star of Fuji House of Commotion and many films
- Advocate for kidney disease awareness and healthcare access; public health campaigner
- Beloved figure in Nigerian popular culture; mentor to younger actresses

chunks.title: Ngozi Nwosu
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Ngozi Nwosu remains a respected and loved figure in Nollywood and a voice for health awareness and care for industry veterans.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Ngozi Nwosu), Nigerian media

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (born 1954, still living) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Modern. Causes: Economic reform, Transparency & anti-corruption, Women's leadership, Global trade & development. Nigerian-American economist who became the first woman and first African Director-General of the WTO. Former Nigerian Finance Minister and World Bank Managing Director. Fun fact: First woman and first African to serve as Director-General of the World Trade Organization

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala was born on 13 June 1954 in Nigeria. She studied economics at Harvard and earned a PhD in regional economics and development from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. She spent 25 years at the World Bank, rising to Managing Director (2007–2011) with responsibility for operations in Africa, South Asia, Europe, and Central Asia.

She served twice as Nigeria's Minister of Finance (2003–2006 and 2011–2015) and briefly as Foreign Minister in 2006, the first woman to hold either post. In March 2021 she became Director-General of the World Trade Organization (WTO), the first woman and first African to lead the WTO.

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Nigeria's economy has been shaped by oil, debt, and governance challenges. Okonjo-Iweala's first term as Finance Minister focused on debt relief, transparency, and reform. Her second term coincided with falling oil prices and security crises; she pushed for fiscal discipline and anti-corruption measures. At the WTO she took office during a pandemic and rising protectionism, with the task of making trade rules more inclusive and effective.

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has worked for sound economic policy, debt sustainability, transparency, and anti-corruption in Nigeria and internationally. She has advocated for women's economic empowerment and for African representation in global institutions. At the WTO she has emphasised development, sustainability, and reform so that trade benefits more people.

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- First woman and first African Director-General of the WTO (2021–)
- Nigeria's first female Finance Minister and first female Foreign Minister
- World Bank Managing Director (2007–2011)
- Led negotiations that secured billions in debt relief for Nigeria
- Named one of Time's 100 most influential people; Forbes among the world's most powerful women
- PhD (MIT); honorary degrees from many universities

chunks.title: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala is a symbol of African and female leadership in global economic governance. Her career links development economics, national policy, and multilateral trade, and she continues to shape debates on trade, development, and inclusion.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala), WTO, World Bank

chunks.title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nike Davies-Okundaye (born 1951, still living) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Art, Women empowerment, Cultural preservation, Education. Nigerian textile artist and cultural icon who turned her own story of survival into a movement. She runs free arts education programmes that have trained over 3,000 Nigerian women and children. Her galleries in Lagos and Osogbo house one of the largest collections of Nigerian art in private hands. She is simply known as Mama Nike. Fun fact: Simply known as 'Mama Nike,' Nike Davies-Okundaye has trained over 3,000 Nigerian women and children through her free arts education programmes.

chunks.title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nike Davies-Okundaye was born in 1951 in Ogidi-Ijumu, Kogi State, Nigeria. Her childhood was marked by hardship. She was married off very young in an arrangement she did not choose, and spent years in extremely difficult circumstances before she was able to leave and build an independent life. She had been trained in traditional Yoruba crafts including adire (resist-dyed cloth), stitching, and weaving from a young age, and it was these skills that gave her a path forward.

She began making and selling textile art. She developed her own distinctive style, combining traditional Yoruba techniques with her own designs. Her work attracted buyers in Nigeria and internationally, and her reputation grew.

She married the artist Twins Seven-Seven in the 1970s and was deeply immersed in the art world that had developed around the Osogbo art movement, a major 20th-century African art movement that emerged from the sacred Osun Grove in Osogbo, Osun State.

She established the Nike Art Gallery in Lagos, and a second gallery and arts centre in Osogbo. Together they house tens of thousands of pieces of Nigerian art and craft work, one of the most significant private collections in the country.

chunks.title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Nike Davies-Okundaye has fought for traditional Nigerian art forms to be treated as serious art and not dismissed as craft or ethnographic curiosity. She has also fought for women and young people from poor backgrounds to have access to artistic education and a way to earn a living through their creativity.

Her arts education programmes are free. She has trained over 3,000 women and children, many of them from economically vulnerable backgrounds, in weaving, batik, embroidery, painting, and other traditional crafts. The goal is always the same: give people skills, and give them economic independence.

She has also been a vocal campaigner for the preservation of Nigerian cultural heritage and has spoken out against the loss of traditional craft knowledge as younger generations move toward urban wage employment.

chunks.title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Founded the Nike Art Gallery in Lagos, home to one of the largest private collections of Nigerian art
- Established the Nike Centre for Art and Culture in Osogbo
- Trained over 3,000 women and children in traditional Nigerian art forms through free programmes
- Recognised internationally as a master artist in Nigerian textile traditions
- Recipient of multiple national and international awards for cultural preservation
- Appointed as an Officer of the Order of the Niger (OON) by the Nigerian government

chunks.title: Nike Davies-Okundaye
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nike Davies-Okundaye has spent her adult life giving away the thing that saved her: art skills and the freedom they bring. Her galleries preserve what might otherwise be lost. Her free training programmes give women the same exit from poverty and dependence that she had to find on her own. She is one of Nigeria's most important cultural figures, and she is still working.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nike Davies-Okundaye), Nike Art Gallery, The Guardian, BBC Africa

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma (born 1949, still living) from South Africa, Southern Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Anti-apartheid activism, Healthcare rights, Women's political leadership, Pan-Africanism. South African politician and physician who served as the first woman Chairperson of the African Union Commission, having previously led South Africa's transformation of its healthcare system as Minister of Health. Fun fact: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma became the first woman ever to chair the African Union Commission.

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nkosazana Clarice Dlamini-Zuma was born on 27 January 1949 in Pietermaritzburg, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. She grew up under apartheid and became politically active as a student, joining the South African Students' Organisation (SASO) and the ANC underground while studying at the University of Zululand.

Forced into exile by the apartheid regime, she completed her medical degree at the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. During her years in exile, she worked in ANC health structures in Swaziland, Mozambique, and Tanzania, providing medical care to refugees and fellow exiles.

After the end of apartheid, she returned to South Africa and entered government, serving in some of the most powerful cabinet positions in the new democracy.

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
South Africa's transition from apartheid to democracy in 1994 required not just political change but the complete transformation of state institutions — including a healthcare system that had been designed to serve the white minority. The new government needed leaders who understood both the technical demands of governance and the political imperatives of the liberation struggle.

At the continental level, the African Union was evolving from a club of heads of state into an institution with ambitions to drive Africa's economic and political integration. The AU Commission chairpersonship became a position of real influence.

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
As South Africa's Minister of Health (1994–1999), Dlamini-Zuma led the overhaul of the apartheid-era healthcare system, expanding primary healthcare access to millions of Black South Africans for the first time. She introduced free healthcare for pregnant women and children under six, and championed the Tobacco Products Control Act, making South Africa a global leader in anti-tobacco legislation.

She later served as Minister of Foreign Affairs (1999–2009), shaping South Africa's post-apartheid foreign policy and its role in African peacekeeping. In 2012, she was elected Chairperson of the African Union Commission — the first woman to hold the position — where she championed Agenda 2063, the AU's long-term development framework.

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- First woman elected Chairperson of the African Union Commission (2012–2017)
- Transformed South Africa's healthcare system as Minister of Health (1994–1999)
- Introduced free healthcare for pregnant women and children under six
- Led South Africa's foreign policy as Minister of Foreign Affairs for a decade
- Championed the AU's Agenda 2063 development framework
- Anti-apartheid activist and exile who served in ANC health structures across Southern Africa

chunks.title: Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma's career spans the full arc of South Africa's modern history — from anti-apartheid resistance to governing a democracy to leading the continent's premier political institution. Her election as AU Commission chair broke a glass ceiling and demonstrated that African women could lead at the highest levels of continental governance.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma), African Union Commission, South African Government archives

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba (1583-1663) from Angola, Central Africa. Era: Pre-Colonial. Causes: Sovereignty & independence, Anti-colonial resistance, Political leadership, Diplomacy & military strategy. Queen of Ndongo and Matamba who resisted Portuguese colonisation and the slave trade for four decades through diplomacy, alliance-building, and military leadership. Fun fact: Fought Portuguese colonisation for 40 years while building alliances across Central Africa

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Nzinga Mbande (also Njinga or Nzingha) was born around 1583 into the royal family of Ndongo, an Ambundu kingdom in what is now northern Angola. Her name is linked to the Kimbundu word kujinga ("to twist or turn"). Legend says she was born with the umbilical cord around her neck. She was trained in politics and warfare and learned to read and write Portuguese from missionaries.

She became a central figure in Ndongo's dealings with the Portuguese. In 1622 she led a diplomatic mission to the Portuguese governor; accounts say she had a servant kneel as her chair to assert equal status. She became queen of Ndongo in 1624 after her brother's death and later ruled the kingdom of Matamba as well.

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: The Portuguese had been on the Angolan coast since the 16th century, seeking slaves and territory. Ndongo and neighbouring kingdoms faced military pressure, slave raids, and political interference. Nzinga ruled in a context of constant negotiation, alliance, and conflict with the Portuguese and with other African powers, including the Imbangala.

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Nzinga fought to preserve Ndongo and Matamba's sovereignty and to limit Portuguese expansion and the slave trade. She used diplomacy, strategic marriages and alliances (including with Imbangala leaders and, for a time, the Dutch), and military force. She led troops into battle and reshaped court and military structures to keep power in her hands. After a long conflict, a peace treaty with Portugal was signed in 1656; she ruled until her death in 1663.

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Queen of Ndongo (1624–1663) and Matamba (1631–1663)
- Resisted Portuguese colonisation and slave-trade expansion for decades
- Formed alliances with the Dutch and Imbangala to counter Portuguese power
- Secured a peace treaty with Portugal in 1656
- Remembered for political skill, military leadership, and diplomatic strength

chunks.title: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Nzinga is a national symbol in Angola and a global icon of African female leadership and resistance to colonialism. Statues, streets, and schools bear her name. UNESCO and others have highlighted her in programmes on women in African history. Her story continues to inspire discussions about gender, power, and resistance in African history.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba), BlackPast.org, Encyclopædia Britannica

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Obiageli Ezekwesili (born 1963, still living) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Education, Anti-corruption, Good governance, Economic development. Nigerian economist, public servant, and global advocate for education and accountability. Co-founder of Transparency International Nigeria, Vice President of the World Bank for Africa, and Nigeria's Federal Minister of Education. Co-launched the BringBackOurGirls campaign in 2014 after the Chibok kidnappings, a global movement that changed how the world talks about violence against girls. Fun fact: Obiageli Ezekwesili co-launched the BringBackOurGirls campaign in 2014, turning the Chibok kidnappings into a global movement that changed how the world talks about violence against girls.

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Obiageli Katryn Ezekwesili (known as Oby) was born on 28 December 1963 in Anambra State, Nigeria. She studied law at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, later earning a master's degree in international law and diplomacy from the University of Lagos, and a master's in public administration from Harvard University's Kennedy School of Government.

She built a career across law, civil society, international development, and government, consistently focused on one question: why do African countries with abundant resources remain poor? Her answer, consistently, has been: corruption, weak institutions, and the failure to invest in people.

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text:
Nigeria in the 1990s and 2000s was grappling with the aftereffects of decades of military rule, widespread corruption, and chronic underinvestment in public services. Transparency International ranked Nigeria among the most corrupt countries in the world. At the same time, structural adjustment programmes, rising debt, and weak governance meant that oil wealth was consistently failing to reach ordinary Nigerians.

Oby Ezekwesili chose to fight that system from the inside, and from the outside.

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
In the late 1990s, Ezekwesili co-founded Transparency International Nigeria, bringing the global anti-corruption network's rigour and tools to Nigeria's civil society at a critical democratic moment.

Under President Olusegun Obasanjo, she served as Special Assistant on Budget Monitoring and Price Intelligence and led the Due Process Office, a mechanism that saved Nigeria billions by scrutinising government contracts for corruption and inflated costs. She brought a prosecutorial energy to government procurement.

She then served as Federal Minister of Solid Minerals Development (2005–2006) and Federal Minister of Education (2006–2007), where she launched reforms aimed at improving school quality, teacher training, and accountability in a vastly underfunded sector.

From 2007 to 2012, she served as Vice President of the World Bank for Africa, one of the most senior positions in the institution, overseeing development lending and policy across the continent.

In April 2014, following the kidnapping of 276 schoolgirls from Government Secondary School Chibok, Borno State, by Boko Haram, Ezekwesili took to the streets of Abuja. She co-founded the BringBackOurGirls campaign, which became a global movement, trended worldwide, and was amplified by everyone from Michelle Obama to Malala Yousafzai. It kept international pressure on the Nigerian government and forced accountability onto what might otherwise have been a forgotten atrocity.

In 2019, she ran for President of Nigeria.

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Co-founded Transparency International Nigeria
- Led Nigeria's Due Process Office, saving billions through procurement reform
- Federal Minister of Education, Nigeria (2006–2007)
- Vice President, World Bank (Africa Region) (2007–2012)
- Co-founded and led the BringBackOurGirls campaign (2014)
- Harvard Kennedy School alumna; multiple honorary degrees
- Presidential candidate, Nigeria, 2019: first major female presidential contender
- Named among Time magazine's 100 Most Influential People

chunks.title: Obiageli Ezekwesili
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Obiageli Ezekwesili remains one of the most prominent advocates for accountability, education, and child rights in Africa. The Chibok girls were never fully returned, but the campaign she helped ignite changed the global conversation around girls' education and Boko Haram's campaign of violence. She continues to speak, write, and campaign, refusing to allow the Nigerian government or the international community to move on.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Obiageli Ezekwesili), World Bank official biography, BringBackOurGirls campaign, Harvard Kennedy School

chunks.title: Olive Schreiner
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Olive Schreiner (1855-1920) from South Africa, Southern Africa. Era: Colonial. Causes: Feminism, Anti-racism, Women's rights, Literature. South African novelist and political activist who wrote The Story of an African Farm in 1883, one of the first great feminist novels in English. She spent her life fighting for women's rights, opposing racism and the Boer War, and insisting that the world she lived in was unjust. Over a century before second-wave feminism, she was already asking the same questions. Fun fact: Olive Schreiner wrote The Story of an African Farm in 1883 — one of the first great feminist novels in English — over a century before second-wave feminism.

chunks.title: Olive Schreiner
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Olive Emilie Albertina Schreiner was born on 24 March 1855 at the Wittebergen mission station in what is now the Eastern Cape, South Africa. She was the ninth of twelve children of a German missionary father and an English mother. She grew up in the harsh landscape of the South African frontier, largely self-educated through voracious reading.

She began writing The Story of an African Farm as a teenager, drawing on the landscape and people around her. She travelled to England in 1881 to try to publish it and, after several rejections, it was published in 1883 under the male pseudonym Ralph Iron. It was an immediate sensation. The novel's protagonist, Lyndall, is one of the most remarkable female characters in Victorian-era fiction: a woman who refuses to accept the role society assigns her, who speaks about gender injustice with a directness that was radical for its time.

She returned to South Africa and became involved in politics. She was a fierce opponent of the Boer War (1899 to 1902), opposing the violence on both sides. She was also a critic of Cecil Rhodes and the racist colonial project in southern Africa. She wrote Woman and Labour (1911), a major feminist text that influenced the suffragette movement in Britain and beyond.

chunks.title: Olive Schreiner
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Schreiner fought against every form of domination she could see: the domination of women by men, of Black people by white colonisers, of subject peoples by empires. She did not pick one cause. She understood them as connected.

She was ahead of her time in almost every direction. She argued for women's sexual autonomy in an era when respectable women were not supposed to have desires. She opposed racism and segregation in a settler colony where those were the foundations of society. She opposed the Boer War when it was popular. She wrote about the inner lives of women at a time when women's inner lives were considered irrelevant.

chunks.title: Olive Schreiner
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Author of The Story of an African Farm (1883), one of the foundational feminist novels in English literature
- Author of Woman and Labour (1911), influential on the suffragette movement internationally
- One of the first major voices to connect feminism and anti-imperialism in African literature
- Her work is studied in literature courses around the world
- The Olive Schreiner Literary Award, South Africa's most prestigious literary prize, is named in her honour

chunks.title: Olive Schreiner
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Olive Schreiner died in 1920, but her questions have not gone away. She asked what women were for and refused to accept the answers she was given. She asked what colonialism was doing to people and refused to look away. She wrote those questions into fiction and political essays that are still read today. She is one of the founding voices of South African literature and African feminism, even though she never used that last word.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Olive Schreiner), The Story of an African Farm (1883), Woman and Labour (1911), South African Literary Awards

chunks.title: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde (born 1978, still living) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Film, Humanitarian work, Women's rights, African storytelling. Nigerian actress and humanitarian who has starred in over 300 films, been named by Time magazine as one of the 100 most influential people in the world, and used her platform to campaign for women and girls across Africa. She is one of the most recognisable faces on the continent and one of Nollywood's greatest stars. Fun fact: With over 300 films to her name, Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde was named by Time magazine as one of the 100 most influential people in the world.

chunks.title: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde was born on 7 February 1978 in Lagos, Nigeria. She began her acting career at 16 and became one of the biggest stars in Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which is the second largest film industry in the world by volume of output.

Over nearly three decades she has starred in more than 300 films, covering a vast range of roles. She is known for the emotional depth she brings to her performances and for consistently choosing roles that explore the real lives and struggles of African women.

Beyond acting, she is a dedicated humanitarian. She has been a UN World Food Programme Ambassador against Hunger, campaigning for food security across Africa. She has also been involved in campaigns against domestic violence, child labour and women's rights abuses.

In 2013, Time magazine included her in its list of the 100 Most Influential People in the World, one of only a handful of Africans to appear on that list. She was listed alongside people including Barack Obama and Beyonce.

chunks.title: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text:
Omotola has used her enormous platform to make the suffering of ordinary Nigerians and Africans visible. She has spoken out about poverty, hunger, violence against women and the exploitation of children. She has visited refugee camps and conflict zones to draw attention to crises that the world was ignoring.

She has also fought for Nollywood to be taken seriously as a cultural and artistic institution, helping to shift perceptions of African filmmaking from cheap entertainment to a powerful storytelling tradition that reflects real African life.

chunks.title: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Over 300 films in a career spanning nearly three decades
- Time magazine 100 Most Influential People in the World (2013)
- UN World Food Programme Ambassador against Hunger
- City of People Award for outstanding contribution to humanity
- Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Actress
- One of Nollywood's most bankable and celebrated stars

chunks.title: Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde is proof that you can be both a great entertainer and a serious advocate. She has used the attention that comes from being one of Africa's most famous actresses to point that attention at things that matter. Generations of Nigerian and African girls have grown up watching her on screen and understanding that a woman can be talented, powerful, beautiful and committed to her community all at once.

---

Sources: Wikipedia (Omotola Jalade-Ekeinde), Time Magazine, UN World Food Programme, Africa Movie Academy Awards

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Omu Okwei (1872-1943) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Colonial. Causes: Women's economic independence, Indigenous African commerce, Women's political authority, Market regulation, Dispute resolution. The 'Merchant Queen of Ossomari': an Igbo trading titan who rose from selling poultry to commanding 20,000 gallons of palm oil, a canoe fleet and vast Onitsha real estate, and was crowned Omu, the last queen of her people's women. Fun fact: She was one of the first people in Onitsha to own a motor car, and she ran a side business renting out her legendary jewellery collection to families for ceremonies.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Okwei was born in 1872 in Ossomari, on the lower Niger River in present-day Anambra State, Nigeria, into Igbo royalty: daughter of Prince Osuna Afubeho, a wealthy warrior who owned trading and war canoes, and granddaughter of King Atanmaya Nzedegwu I of Ossomari. She had no formal schooling; at nine her mother sent her to live with Igala relatives, where she learned to trade fruits, yams and poultry. In 1889 she married Joseph Allagoa, a trader from Brass, against her family's wishes (they considered a trader beneath her royal rank), and though the marriage ended around 1890, it introduced her to European traders and African middlemen, connections she leveraged to start her own poultry trade. In 1895 she married Opene of Aboh, whose mother was herself a wealthy trader, and partnered with her mother-in-law before striking out on her own.

In 1904 she became an agent of the Niger Company, trading palm oil for European goods, one of very few African women in such a position. At her peak she held 400 trading "tickets," roughly 20,000 gallons of palm oil. During and after the First World War she diversified into tobacco, cotton goods, ivory and coral beads, plus money-lending to smaller traders and extensive real estate: she came to own canoe fleets, trucks and over a third of the riverside land at Onitsha. From 1912 into the 1930s she served on the Onitsha Native Court, one of the few women with a formal voice in colonial-era adjudication.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Biography (2)
chunks.text: In August 1935 she was crowned Omu (Queen) of Ossomari, head of the Council of Mothers in the Igbo "dual-sex" governance system, responsible for women's affairs, markets and dispute settlement, with official residences in both Ossomari and Onitsha. Her network-building had a harder edge history should not gloss: she acquired pawned girls whom she placed as wives and mistresses of influential businessmen to extend her commercial reach, a practice of her era that modern readers must weigh honestly alongside her achievements. She died in 1943 in Onitsha, leaving about £5,000 in the bank and twenty-four houses. No Omu of Ossomari has been crowned since.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Okwei's lifetime spans the British conquest and consolidation of Southern Nigeria: the Royal Niger Company era, the 1900 transfer to Crown rule, and full colonial administration. European firms monopolised import-export trade, making African intermediaries like Okwei indispensable. Igbo polities such as Ossomari traditionally practised "dual-sex" government, with a male Obi and a female Omu ruling women's spheres, an institution the British ignored and eroded. Okwei was its last great holder in Ossomari.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: Economic power for African women within a colonial economy stacked against them. She proved that an Igbo woman could out-trade the intermediary class, bank the profits, and convert wealth into institutional authority. As Omu she defended women's traditional political power (the Council of Mothers, the markets, the right of women to govern their own commercial world) even as colonial rule was dismantling the very idea.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Became an agent of the Niger Company in 1904, one of very few African women in such a position.
- Reached a peak trade of 400 tickets, roughly 20,000 gallons of palm oil, ranking among the wealthiest traders on the lower Niger.
- Appointed to the Onitsha Native Court in 1912, serving into the 1930s.
- Pioneered money-lending to smaller traders and built an empire of canoe fleets, trucks and Onitsha real estate.
- Crowned Omu of Ossomari in August 1935, the last person ever to hold the title.
- Died in 1943 leaving twenty-four houses in Onitsha and £5,000, an enormous estate for the time.

chunks.title: Omu Okwei
chunks.heading: Her Impact Today
chunks.text:
Celebrated as Nigeria's "Merchant Queen," Okwei is a staple of Nigerian women's history, the standing proof that female enterprise on the Niger predated and outmanoeuvred colonialism. A statue marks her burial site at Ugolo Village, Ossomala, and her story anchors scholarship on the Igbo dual-sex political system: a reminder that African women once held constitutional power that colonial rule erased, and that its memory is itself a form of resistance.

---

Sources: F. I. Ekejiuba, "Omu Okwei, the Merchant Queen of Ossomari" (Journal of the Historical Society of Nigeria, 1967), Wikipedia (Omu Okwei), Encyclopedia.com (Women in World History), Smithsonian Institution Libraries catalogue.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: Profile
chunks.text: Onyeka Onwenu (1952-2024) from Nigeria, West Africa. Era: Contemporary. Causes: Women's empowerment, HIV/AIDS awareness, National unity, Niger Delta environmental justice, Artists' rights. Nigeria's 'Elegant Stallion': singer, journalist, actress and public servant whose hit songs preached unity and family planning, whose 1984 documentary indicted oil corruption, and who spent a lifetime refusing to stay in one lane. Fun fact: She collapsed minutes after performing at Stella Okoli's 80th birthday celebration in 2024, and in a 2021 essay she had already instructed that her burial be done 'quickly, quietly and privately', saying celebrations should happen while she was alive to enjoy them.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: Biography
chunks.text:
Onyeka Onwenu was born on 31 January 1952 in Obosi and raised in Port Harcourt, with family roots in Arondizuogu, Imo State. Her father, the educationist and politician D. K. Onwenu, died in a road accident when she was four, a week before he was to be appointed Minister for Education, leaving her mother Hope to raise five children alone after in-laws denied her access to his property. Onyeka studied International Relations and Communication at Wellesley College in Massachusetts, took a Master's in Media Studies at The New School in New York, and worked at the United Nations before returning to Nigeria in 1980 for national service with the Nigerian Television Authority, where she became a newsreader and reporter.

She launched a parallel music career in 1981 with "For the Love of You," followed through the decade by "Endless Life," "In the Morning Light," "One Love" and "Dancing in the Sun." Her duets with the Yoruba juju king Sunny Adé, most famously "Wait for Me," recorded for a family-planning campaign, became Igbo-Yoruba unity anthems in a country still healing from civil war. As a journalist she wrote and presented the landmark 1984 BBC and NTA documentary "Nigeria: A Squandering of Riches," widely called the definitive film on Nigerian corruption and Niger Delta environmental degradation. In 2000 she staged a hunger strike outside NTA headquarters over unpaid royalties for her song "Iyogogo," dragging artists' rights into the national conversation.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: Biography (2)
chunks.text: From 1999 she added Nollywood to her portfolio, winning the 2006 Africa Movie Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for "Widow's Cot" and appearing in more than thirty films, including "Half of a Yellow Sun" and "Lionheart." She judged X Factor Nigeria, chaired the Imo State Council for Arts and Culture, and in 2013 was appointed Executive Director of the National Centre for Women Development. She published her autobiography, "My Father's Daughter," in 2021. On 30 July 2024 she collapsed shortly after performing at the 80th birthday celebration of Emzor Pharmaceuticals founder Stella Okoli in Lagos, and was pronounced dead at 72.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: Historical Context
chunks.text: Her life tracked Nigeria's arc: an Igbo childhood interrupted by the civil war, the oil boom and bust her 1984 documentary indicted, military rule and democratic transitions in which she took political roles, and the rise of Nollywood and Afropop that she helped legitimise for women. She modelled a kind of public womanhood Nigeria had not seen: glamorous, learned, fearless and impossible to categorise.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: What She Fought For
chunks.text: The dignity of Nigerian women in public life; honest reckoning with corruption and the ruin of the Niger Delta; HIV/AIDS awareness and family planning delivered through popular music; fair pay for artists; and national unity built through cross-ethnic collaboration, one duet at a time.

chunks.title: Onyeka Onwenu
chunks.heading: Major Achievements
chunks.text:
- Wrote and presented the BBC/NTA documentary "Nigeria: A Squandering of Riches" (1984).
- A string of hit albums through the 1980s, including landmark unity duets with King Sunny Adé.
- High-profile royalties protest and hunger strike against NTA that advanced artists' rights in Nigeria (2000).
